1-11.cost: A set of window guards or child-safety locks costs about ₹500–₹1,500 to buy and install, and the job takes about ten minutes.

1-14.inPlainWords: The test itself is very inexpensive. In the Qidong 30-year follow-up study, infants who received the hepatitis B vaccine at birth had an 84% lower risk of developing primary liver cancer and a 72% lower rate of carrying the hepatitis B virus than unvaccinated peers. An adult found to have no antibodies needs three doses over six months.
1-14.caveats: This recommendation is for adults who were never vaccinated as a child, or whose antibodies have waned. India ran a hepatitis B vaccination pilot in ten states from 2002–03 and added the vaccine to the routine infant schedule nationally only in 2011, so most adults born before that were not vaccinated at birth and should check their status rather than assume they are covered. The 84% cancer-risk reduction belongs to people immunised at birth; adolescents vaccinated later saw only a 21% fall in virus carriage. For an adult the aim is to prevent a new infection, not to reproduce that cancer benefit. Vaccination does nothing for someone already infected; they need regular follow-up with a hepatologist. Infection is confirmed when the hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) test is positive, and a full panel tells you whether you are immune, infected or susceptible.
1-14.cost: The test costs just a few hundred rupees per person. For adults lacking antibodies, three doses of the hepatitis B vaccine are given over six months; the course price varies with the brand, so ask the clinic for the total before you start.

1-15.cost: A clinic visit and wound cleaning cost about ₹300–₹800. If a tetanus vaccine or immunoglobulin is needed, add about ₹1,000–₹5,000 depending on the product and the hospital.
1-15.sources: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Tetanus: "Tetanus bacteria can get into someone's body through broken skin, usually through injuries.""Tetanus can lead to death (1 in 10 cases in the United States are fatal).""People who didn't complete the primary series or who aren't up to date with their 10-year tetanus booster shots are also at increased risk.""Vaccination also helps prevent tetanus in people with wounds, depending on their tetanus vaccination history."<https://www.cdc.gov/tetanus/about/index.html>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>; World Health Organization. <https://www.who.int/>

1-25.title: Call Tele-MANAS on 14416 if you are depressed or having suicidal thoughts; do not keep sleeping pills or pesticides at home
1-25.cost: There’s no cost involved. You just need to make one phone call. Plus, lock away any medications and keep pesticides out of the house.
1-25.inPlainWords: Removing lethal items from easy reach is a proven way to cut suicide risk: after restricting access to painkillers, suicide rates linked to them dropped by 43%; installing barriers at locations where people often jump off cliffs cut rates by 86%. That’s why it’s a good idea to avoid storing sleeping pills and pesticides at home. If you’re feeling overwhelmed, call 14416 (Tele-MANAS) — this helpline answers 24 hours a day, every day.
1-25.benefit: A recent review of nearly a decade’s worth of research confirms that limiting people’s access to lethal means is an effective suicide prevention strategy. After controls on painkiller availability were put in place, suicide cases tied to these drugs fell by 43%. Installing protective barriers at common suicide hotspots reduced rates by 86% (the 95% confidence interval ranges from 79% to 91%). School-based cognitive intervention programs also lowered rates of attempted suicide by roughly 55% (OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.24–0.85). Antidepressant medications and psychotherapy are also key components of suicide prevention.
1-25.sources: Zalsman G et al. (2016). Suicide prevention strategies revisited: 10-year systematic review. Lancet Psychiatry. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S2215-0366(16)30030-X>; Tele-MANAS, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://telemanas.mohfw.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>
1-25.caveats: The B rating is based on two factors: most evidence supporting restrictive measures comes from ecological studies that compare suicide rates before and after policy implementation; there is currently no direct evidence that the helpline itself reduces overall mortality rates. Suicidal impulses typically last only a few minutes to a few hours, so simply removing lethal items from immediate reach is a meaningful intervention on its own. Data on outcomes over longer time periods following suicide attempts, as well as information on long-term consequences for survivors, can be found in Chapter 1, Item 32 (“Tell someone close to you as soon as suicidal thoughts arise”).

1-27.cost: A routine urine test costs a few hundred rupees at most labs, and an ultrasound of the urinary tract costs more; ask the centre for its price. If the doctor advises a cystoscopy, it costs considerably more at a private hospital than at a government one.

1-31.title: If you have engaged in high-risk behaviour, get tested for HIV — government testing is free and confidential
1-31.inPlainWords: The HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017 keeps your HIV status confidential: anyone who learns it through testing, treatment or counselling may not pass it on without your informed consent. A positive result does not mean a death sentence: people who take treatment and keep their viral load undetectable cannot transmit the virus to sexual partners. One major study followed more than 700 couples through over 70,000 unprotected acts; there were zero transmissions between partners.
1-31.benefit: Testing is free and confidential at the government Integrated Counselling and Testing Centres run under the National AIDS Control Programme in every district, and pre-test counselling is part of the visit. Early detection is far more than a psychological comfort — antiretroviral therapy can drive the virus down to undetectable levels, and first-line treatment is free at government centres. The World Health Organization states that individuals on such treatment with an undetectable viral load pose no risk of HIV transmission. The PARTNER study observed 782 same-sex couples (serodiscordant pairs) for a total of 1,593 person-years; despite 76,088 unprotected encounters, only 15 new infections occurred, and genetic analysis proved none originated from the partner. The Act also bars any person who holds HIV-related information from disclosing it without informed consent, except in the narrow cases it lists, such as a court order.
1-31.caveats: The “window period” is a property of the test, not of the infection: a nucleic-acid test can detect HIV after roughly one week, a fourth-generation antigen-antibody test after about two weeks, and a third-generation antibody-only test after three weeks. No Indian agency publishes an official table of window periods, so these figures come from the assay makers and from WHO. It is advisable to wait at least two weeks post-exposure and then retest after another two to four weeks; after three months, 99.99% of people can be certain they are not infected. The Act prohibits discrimination against people living with HIV and their families in employment, education, healthcare, housing and public facilities, and requires that they be treated like anyone else. It also obliges a person diagnosed with HIV to take reasonable precautions to prevent transmission, while protecting their right to keep their status confidential; compelling a partner disclosure is not the mechanism the Act uses. Screening for HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B during pregnancy and related prevention measures are covered in Chapter 27.
1-31.sources: Rodger AJ, Cambiano V, Bruun T, et al. (2019). Risk of HIV transmission through condomless sex in serodifferent gay couples with the HIV-positive partner taking suppressive antiretroviral therapy (PARTNER): final results of a multicentre, prospective, observational study. benefit: Starting May 1, 2025, China launched a nationwide mental health hotline at 12356, available at least 18 hours per day.

1-6.inPlainWords: Do not push an electric scooter or e-bike into a stairwell or lift, and do not charge it inside your home. A lithium-ion battery can catch fire within seconds and fill a stairwell with toxic smoke, cutting off your only escape route. Charge at a designated outdoor point, use the charger supplied with the vehicle, and never leave a battery charging overnight.
1-6.benefit: The National Building Code and the state fire-safety rules require common areas and escape routes to stay clear. The BIS standard for lithium-ion batteries and chargers is a safety baseline; a cheap unbranded battery may not meet it. A charging fire in a lobby or stairwell is especially dangerous because smoke rises and the exit is blocked. Many apartment associations now ban indoor charging in their bye-laws.
1-6.cost: No direct cost. The inconvenience is walking to the designated charging point. A BIS-certified charger and battery cost more than an unbranded one.
1-6.caveats: Do not buy a modified battery or a generic charger. Do not charge a damaged battery. If a battery swells, heats up or smells, stop using it and take it to a service centre.
1-6.sources: Bureau of Indian Standards, lithium-ion battery standards. <https://www.bis.gov.in/>; National Disaster Management Authority, fire safety. <https://ndma.gov.in/>; Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. <https://mohua.gov.in/>

1-2.cost: A helmet costs from a few hundred rupees to a few thousand, depending on the standard it meets, and takes five seconds to put on each time.

1-3.cost: A smoke alarm costs a few hundred rupees and a carbon monoxide alarm a few thousand. After installation, the batteries need to be replaced once a year.

1-10.cost: A child car seat costs a few thousand rupees and lasts several years. It adds about one minute to each trip to buckle the child in.

1-12.cost: Life jackets cost from a few hundred to a few thousand rupees. Parents must also give constant attention to watching their children.
1-12.inPlainWords: Wearing a life jacket while in the water cuts the risk of drowning to roughly half compared to not wearing one.
1-12.benefit: Research using U.S. Coast Guard data compared similar groups of people. For individuals who fell overboard while boating recreationally, wearing a life jacket lowered their drowning risk by about half. The unadjusted RR was 0.51, with a 95% CI of 0.35–0.74. Drowning remains one of the leading causes of death in childhood. The World Health Organization estimates around 300,000 drowning deaths a year worldwide; children under 5 account for nearly a quarter of them; drowning is the fourth leading cause of death for children aged 1–4 years and the third for children aged 5–14 years; and 92% of drowning deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries.
1-12.sources: Cummings P et al. (2011). Association between wearing a personal floatation device and death by drowning among recreational boaters. Injury Prevention. <https://doi.org/10.1136/ip.2010.028688>; World Health Organization (2026). Drowning [fact sheet, 1 May 2026]. <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/drowning> (accessed 21 October 2026)

1-18.cost: An HPV test at a private laboratory typically costs a few thousand rupees, and the sampling takes a few minutes; government facilities generally charge less. A woman with a negative result can be tested again only once every five years.
1-18.inPlainWords: In that rural Indian trial, women who underwent just one HPV test in their lifetime had roughly half the risk of dying from cervical cancer and about 50% lower odds of being diagnosed with advanced-stage disease. At a cost of a few thousand rupees per test, a negative result provides protection for five years.

1-4.title: Replace the gas hose and regulator when they are due, never tamper with the piping yourself, and refuse unsolicited “safety” sales visits
1-4.cost: A compliant hose costs a few hundred rupees and a regulator rather more; a stove is replaced when the maker’s service life ends. The job takes one visit from an authorised mechanic, and the replacement date is printed on the hose itself.
1-4.inPlainWords: The rubber tube between an LPG cylinder and the stove hardens, cracks and leaks as it ages, and a leaking joint is the ordinary way a kitchen fire starts. In India the hose and the regulator carry a printed date and a replacement interval, and changing them on time is the owner’s job. Under the Gas Cylinders Rules, 2016, only cylinders and fittings approved by the Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation may be used. The safety instructions that come with the connection from the oil marketing companies add that the tubing should be of an approved grade, kept as short as the distance allows, and not run through a wall or under a door. If you have piped natural gas instead, the connection and the internal line may be installed or altered only by the city gas distribution company authorised by the Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board; nobody else should touch it.
1-4.benefit: These rules exist because a perished hose, a worn regulator washer or a joint that was never checked can turn a small leak into a fire, and because a cylinder refilled or repaired outside the licensed system carries no test record. Replacing the hose and regulator at the interval printed on them, keeping the tube away from heat, and checking the joints with soap solution now and then removes the commonest failure points. No rule obliges you to buy a hose, a regulator, a stove or an alarm from your distributor or from anyone who turns up at the door.
1-4.sources: Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board. <https://pngrb.gov.in/>; Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation, Gas Cylinders Rules, 2016. <https://peso.gov.in/>; Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. <https://mopng.gov.in/>; Bureau of Indian Standards, IS 4384, rubber hoses for liquefied petroleum gas. <https://www.bis.gov.in/>
1-4.caveats: People pose as gas inspectors, perform a perfunctory “check” and then sell self-closing valves, alarms or hoses at a mark-up. You may refuse, and you may complain to the distributor or to the oil marketing company. If you smell gas: shut the cylinder valve, open the doors and windows, do not switch any electrical switch on or off, including lights and exhaust fans, do not light a flame, and leave the house. Call the 24-hour emergency number printed on the cylinder or the consumer card — every oil marketing company runs an LPG emergency line — or the city gas distribution emergency number for piped gas, from outside. A headache, nausea or drowsiness in the house at the same time is carbon monoxide poisoning until proved otherwise; get everyone out and to a hospital. See Chapter 13.

1-5.title: Do not pick, buy or eat wild mushrooms; no folk test tells a poisonous one from a safe one
1-5.cost: No expense involved. The hard part is giving up a seasonal delicacy, and the argument with the relative who picked it.
1-5.inPlainWords: No Indian agency publishes a nationwide count of wild-mushroom poisonings, so any figure you read online is a partial tally. The pattern that does repeat is a household cooking one pot from a day’s picking and several people falling ill together, often hours later. Testing with a silver needle, cooking with garlic, assuming a mushroom is safe because insects have eaten it, or believing that only brightly coloured ones are toxic are all false tests.
1-5.benefit: The danger is not an upset stomach but liver and kidney failure. The species that carry amatoxins cause vomiting and diarrhoea that seem to settle after a day, and liver injury follows two or three days later — which is why people reach hospital too late. Cooking does not destroy amatoxins, and a mushroom that one adult has eaten without harm is not therefore safe for a child, a pregnant woman or an older adult. Identification turns on features most pickers cannot see, and species new to science are described every year, so there is no home test worth trusting.
1-5.caveats: If anyone has eaten a suspect mushroom, go to a hospital at once and take the leftovers, the trimmings, or photographs of what was picked and where. Do not wait for the stomach upset to pass: the quiet day that follows is part of the poisoning, not the end of it. Treatment differs by toxin, so identifying the species matters. “Local people know them” is not a safe assumption, and neither is any of the folk tests above.
1-5.sources: White J, Weinstein SA, De Haro L, et al. (2019). Mushroom poisoning: a proposed new clinical classification. Toxicon, 157, 53-65.; Indian Council of Medical Research. <https://www.icmr.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>

1-9.title: Do not speed or drive after drinking, keep off the phone, and pull over to rest when you are tired
1-9.cost: There is no direct cost. Driving a little slower adds a few minutes to a trip. The hard part is drinking less at a social gathering and leaving the phone alone. On a long drive, plan a break of at least 20 minutes every few hours.
1-9.inPlainWords: On average, every 1% rise in speed raises the chance of a fatal crash by about 4%. There is no blood alcohol level at which driving is safe. Handling a phone while driving makes a crash about 3.6 times more likely than attentive driving, and dialling raises it 12.2 times. A driver who is visibly tired runs about 3.4 times the crash risk.
1-9.benefit: The World Health Organization puts the speed relationship at a 1% rise in average speed producing a 4% rise in fatal crash risk, and reports that risk climbs from the lowest blood alcohol concentrations. WHO also reports that drivers using a phone are about four times more likely to crash than those who are not, and that hands-free sets offer little advantage. A naturalistic study with cameras in more than 3,500 vehicles compared 905 injury and property-damage crashes with baseline alert, attentive, sober driving: handling a handheld phone raised crash odds 3.6-fold, dialling 12.2-fold, texting or messaging 6.1-fold, reaching for the device 4.8-fold, browsing 2.7-fold and handheld conversation 2.2-fold. Observable fatigue and drowsiness raised crash risk 3.4-fold (odds ratio 3.4).
1-9.caveats: The 1% speed and 4% fatality ratio comes from traffic modelling, not from randomised trials. For alcohol, WHO describes an upward trend with no fixed harmless threshold. The phone and drowsiness odds ratios cover all injury and property-damage crashes, not fatal crashes alone, and the baseline was ideal attentive driving, which inflates the ratios a little. Indian law penalises drink-driving under section 185 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and dangerous driving under section 184; it sets no statutory rest break for a private driver, so the four-hour guidance here is advice, not a legal rule. Commercial passenger and goods vehicles run to permit conditions and state rules, so if you drive for a living, check what your permit requires. If you are drowsy, pull over at a fuel station and sleep. Sedating antihistamines such as chlorpheniramine or diphenhydramine also impair driving markedly, as Chapter 34, Rule 12 sets out. Persistent drowsiness at the wheel with loud snoring is worth a sleep-apnoea assessment, described in Chapter 3, Rule 27.
1-9.sources: World Health Organization (2025). Road traffic injuries fact sheet. <https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/road-traffic-injuries>; Dingus TA et al. (2016). Driver crash risk factors and prevalence evaluation using naturalistic driving data. 1-45.cost: An anti-HCV antibody test costs a few hundred rupees at a private laboratory and is free or nominal at a government hospital under the National Viral Hepatitis Control Programme. If it is positive, an HCV RNA PCR test shows whether the infection is active. Treatment is a direct-acting antiviral taken as one tablet a day for 8 to 12 weeks, free at designated government hospitals under the same programme and available as low-cost generics in the private market. The real obstacle is that a person with no symptoms rarely thinks to be tested.

1-26.cost: A set of fire extinguishers, fire blankets, one escape respirator per person and a first-aid kit costs a few thousand rupees, and it is bought once. After that, inspecting the items takes about 10 minutes a year.
1-26.inPlainWords: A fire extinguisher, a fire blanket, an escape respirator and a first-aid kit are the core of a household emergency kit. India has no single government list of household emergency supplies, but the Bureau of Indian Standards sets the standard each item is made to, and the ISI mark on an extinguisher shows it was type-tested. The set is bought once and takes about ten minutes a year to check. Studies of home safety programmes that included on-site guidance found these measures cut injury rates by roughly 25%.
1-26.benefit: A home emergency kit is built around four items. A fire extinguisher and a fire blanket are for putting out a small fire at its start, and the blanket can be draped over a person to help them get out. An escape respirator is designed to be worn on the way out of a smoke-filled room, not to fight the fire. The first-aid box holds dressings, bandages and antiseptic for treating a wound. In India, portable extinguishers are made and tested to the Bureau of Indian Standards specification and carry the ISI mark, and a pressure gauge on the cylinder shows whether it is still charged. Cochrane analysed 98 studies involving 2,605,044 participants in total. Home safety interventions lowered injury rates to an IRR of 0.89; the 95% confidence interval for this figure is 0.78 to 1.01. For interventions that included on-site guidance, injury rates dropped by around 25% (IRR 0.75, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.91).
1-26.caveats: This finding is somewhat controversial. The same Cochrane meta-analysis found that interventions that did not provide emergency supplies also lowered injury rates by roughly 20%. The original IRR for those interventions was 0.78, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.66 to 0.92. Providing emergency supplies alone did not yield better results than other measures. The main effect of these interventions comes from on-site education and home modifications, so the benefit of supplying emergency supplies is rated as “moderate” rather than “significant”. When buying a fire extinguisher, look for the ISI mark and check that the pressure gauge needle points to the green zone. Details on smoke alarms and carbon monoxide detectors are covered in Rule 3 of this chapter. Instructions for using tourniquets can be found in Chapter 13, Rule 12. Ask the supplier how each item is refilled or replaced, and what its service life is.

1-33.title: Don’t treat “survival” as a safety net: after ingesting paraquat or inhaling carbon monoxide, emergency care can save lives, but it rarely preserves lung or brain function.
1-33.cost: No cost involved. It simply helps you understand this reality up front.
1-33.inPlainWords: There is no antidote for paraquat. Gastric lavage is not recommended, and neither hemofiltration nor dialysis alters its disease progression. Paraquat actively enters lung tissue against its concentration gradient, causing pneumonia and pulmonary fibrosis, while also damaging kidneys and liver. Among 257 cases treated at ten hospitals in Bangladesh, the mortality rate reached 43.2%. Carbon monoxide produces similar outcomes: six weeks after exposure, 46.1% of patients receiving normal oxygen still suffered cognitive impairment, compared to 25.0% of those receiving hyperbaric oxygen therapy. No treatment pathway yields a completely clean outcome; the most common result is lasting health complications.
1-33.benefit: A systematic review on paraquat poisoning highlights its extremely high mortality rate, stemming from its intrinsic toxicity and lack of effective treatments. Paraquat is actively transported into lung tissue against its concentration gradient, resulting in pneumonia, pulmonary fibrosis, kidney and liver damage. The review explicitly advises against gastric lavage; hemofiltration and dialysis are unlikely to alter clinical outcomes. Evidence supporting corticosteroids or immunosuppressants remains weak. It also notes that mortality rates remain high across all centers despite varying treatment approaches. In Bangladesh, 1,420 cases were reported to ten tertiary hospitals between 2013 and 2024; full data were available for 257 of them, and the case fatality rate in that group was 43.2%. Common symptoms included lower limb swelling due to acute kidney failure (71.2%), vomiting (65.8%) and abdominal pain (58.0%). Another randomized, double-blind trial involving 76 patients per group examined acute carbon monoxide poisoning; six weeks later, 25.0% of those receiving hyperbaric oxygen therapy and 46.1% of those receiving normal oxygen still had cognitive impairments (P=0.007; adjusted OR 0.45, 95% CI 0.22–0.92). A separate study of 73 patients found 30% developed cognitive impairments and 12% showed hyperintense signals in white matter on brain imaging. India has now moved against paraquat. By Order S.O. 5234(E) dated 22 September 2026, issued under section 27(2) read with section 28 of the Insecticides Act, 1968 and published in the Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II, Section 3(ii), on 23 September 2026 (CG-DL-E-28092026-276542), the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare prohibited any further registration of paraquat dichloride and cancelled every certificate of registration granted for it under section 9 of the Act from the date of publication, after an intention notice, S.O. 3800(E), of 10 July 2026. The Registration Committee is to call the certificates back, and the state governments are to enforce the order under the Act. That stops new registration and cancels the licences; stock already with dealers, and the pace of state enforcement, are separate questions, so the poisoning described here remains a live risk in India for now.

British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology, 72(5), 745-757. <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2125.2011.04026.x>; Weaver LK, Hopkins RO, Chan KJ, et al. (2002). Hyperbaric oxygen for acute carbon monoxide poisoning. New England Journal of Medicine, 347(14), 1057-1067. <https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa013121>; Parkinson RB, Hopkins RO, Cleavinger HB, et al. (2002). White matter hyperintensities and neuropsychological outcome following carbon monoxide poisoning. Neurology, 58(10), 1525-1532. <https://doi.org/10.1212/WNL.58.10.1525>; Chowdhury FR et al. (2026). Clinical and Laboratory Profile of Paraquat Poisoning: A Toxicological Crisis in Bangladesh. 1-33.caveats: Grade B is assigned because these studies involve general poisoning patients rather than solely suicide attempt survivors; the carbon monoxide trial even included accidental poisoning cases. Consequently, observed complication rates cannot be directly interpreted as probabilities specific to suicide attempts. This entry does not compare mortality rates across different treatment methods nor recommend any specific actions. The sole certainty is that no treatment pathway guarantees a completely clean outcome. On-site management of carbon monoxide poisoning is detailed in Chapter 13, Item 19. For accidental ingestion of pesticides or medications, avoid inducing vomiting and seek medical help while bringing the container along (Chapter 13, Item 20). Finally, refrain from storing pesticides or sedatives at home (Chapter 1, Item 25). The text of the order was read from a copy of Gazette issue CG-DL-E-28092026-276542; the official eGazette portal could not be reached when this chapter was checked on 21 October 2026, so confirm the current position with the Central Insecticides Board and Registration Committee (cibrc.nic.in) before relying on it.

1-46.inPlainWords: Septic tanks, manholes, cesspools, and sealed vegetable cellars accumulate lethal concentrations of toxic gases (like hydrogen sulfide) and suffer severe oxygen deficiency, knocking an entrant unconscious within seconds. Across official industrial accident registries, a single worker collapses, and coworkers or relatives rush in consecutively to rescue them, only to die alongside them. Official statistics show over half of all confined space fatalities are would-be rescuers. If someone collapses inside, never enter: call 112 (the single emergency number, which reaches ambulance, fire and police) immediately.
1-46.benefit:
A "confined space" refers to enclosed or partially enclosed spaces not designed for continuous human occupancy, including septic tanks, sewage pits, manholes, storage cellars, and industrial vats. The U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) investigated 70 fatal confined space incidents between 1983 and 1993 involving 109 deaths: 39 victims (36%) entered specifically to rescue others, and only 4 of those 39 were trained emergency personnel. A 1986 NIOSH alert estimated that approximately 60% of confined space fatalities were would-be rescuers.

India has no single regulation covering confined-space entry in homes, farms and small workshops; the duty is split between statutes. Until 21 November 2025 the rule for a factory was section 36 of the Factories Act, 1948: nobody could be required or allowed to enter a tank, pit, pipe, flue or similar confined space where gas, fume, vapour or dust may be present until all practicable measures had been taken to remove the danger and a competent person had certified in writing, on the basis of a test, that the space was reasonably free of dangerous gas — or the entrant was wearing suitable breathing apparatus. In practice that was ventilate, test, then enter, written into law. That Act was repealed on 21 November 2025, when the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 came into force, and section 143 of the Code is the repeal provision. The Code does not restate section 36 word for word; what it imposes is a general employer duty. Section 6 requires every employer to ensure that the workplace is free from hazards which cause or are likely to cause injury or occupational disease, to provide and maintain plant and systems of work that are safe and without risk to health, and to provide information, instruction, training and supervision. Section 23 requires the employer to maintain the health, safety and working conditions prescribed under the Code, including ventilation and an environment free from dust, noxious gas and fumes. The detail is left to rules made under the Code and to each state's rules, so the practice is unchanged — ventilate, test, then enter, with breathing apparatus if the test cannot clear the space — but the law to cite now is the Code and its rules, not section 36 of the 1948 Act. For sewers and septic tanks a second statute applies: section 7 of the Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013 bars any person, local authority or agency from employing anyone, directly or indirectly, for hazardous cleaning of a sewer or a septic tank, and the NAMASTE scheme (National Action for Mechanised Sanitation Ecosystem) is the government programme that replaces manual entry with machines and trained crews.

Safety manuals explain that while hydrogen sulfide smells like rotten eggs at low levels, high concentrations rapidly cause olfactory paralysis—the human nose completely loses the ability to smell it. Concentrations exceeding 1,000 mg/m³ cause instantaneous "knockdown" and death within seconds. Similarly, extreme carbon dioxide concentrations induce loss of consciousness in seconds. Emergency guidelines are equally blunt: if the people on site have no breathing apparatus and no retrieval gear, call 112 (or 108 for an ambulance), and under no circumstances should forced entry be attempted. A rescue from outside is only possible if the entrant was already wearing a full-body harness attached to an external retrieval line.

Unventilated subterranean vegetable cellars pose the same acute asphyxiation risk, because stored root vegetables consume oxygen and release dense carbon dioxide; open every hatch and let the cellar air for a long time, test the air, wear a safety rope, and keep someone on the surface watching before anyone goes down.
1-46.caveats: Grade C is assigned because data stem from occupational casualty registries and safety engineering codes rather than clinical intervention trials. Benefit magnitude is rated Moderate: while the event outcome is frequently fatal (often taking multiple lives at once), exposure is concentrated among individuals who access these subterranean structures. Common domestic encounters include cleaning septic or biogas tanks and descending into winter vegetable storage cellars. Never rely on smell to judge atmospheric safety; absence of odor does not mean toxic gas is absent. If an employer assigns work in a shaft or tank without mechanical ventilation, gas testing, continuous surface monitoring or a safety harness, raise it with the employer before entering and, if nothing changes, report it to the Inspector-cum-Facilitator appointed under the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, or to the state labour department. If someone collapses inside, shout for help and dial 112 (ambulance 108); external actions are limited to removing covers and using fans or blowers from outside. Once an unconscious victim is extracted to fresh air, check for breathing and initiate chest compressions if breathing is absent, as outlined in Chapter 13, Item 1. The protocol remains identical whether the victim is a coworker, neighbor, or stranger, adhering to the same safety boundary as Chapter 13, Item 25 (do not jump into water if you see someone drowning). Carbon monoxide risks from indoor fuel burning are covered in Chapter 1, Item 3. Primary beneficiaries are yourself (as the prospective rescuer) and coworkers or family members.

1-48.inPlainWords: Black fungus and tremella (silver ear) soaked for hours, fresh wet rice noodles kept at room temperature, and home-fermented corn flour can all grow a bacterium, Burkholderia gladioli pathovar cocovenenans, that produces bongkrekic acid, a lethal toxin. It cannot be broken down by 100°C boiling or pressure cooking, and no medical antidote exists. Indian kitchens ferment rice, dal and corn, and leftover soaked fungus or noodles are common, so the risk is preparative habit rather than any particular dish.
1-48.benefit: Bongkrekic acid is produced when oil-rich plant material is fermented in warm conditions, or when wet rice noodles stand at room temperature for hours. It is heat-stable and resistant to boiling and pressure cooking, and no specific antidote exists; care is supportive — fluids, and intensive care for the severe cases, which are often fatal. The risk sits in everyday practice: a batch of home-fermented corn or rice left standing through a hot afternoon, wet rice noodles or soaked fungus kept outside the refrigerator, and fungus soaked far longer than the recipe needs. FSSAI's contaminant regulations set limits for packaged food and require manufacturers to control the hazard, but a batch fermented or soaked at home is outside any inspection, so the only control is the one you apply in your own kitchen.
1-48.caveats: Dried black fungus requires only 1 to 2 hours of cold-water soaking; market guidelines stipulate soaking should never exceed 8 hours. If soaked fungus feels slimy, loses elasticity, gives off a sour or unpleasant odor, or the soaking water turns turbid, discard the whole batch. If vomiting, dizziness or profound weakness appear after eating, do not wait to see how it goes: go to a hospital emergency department immediately and take the leftover food or its container with you. Anyone who shared the meal should be medically evaluated even if they feel well so far. Wild toxic mushrooms are covered in Rule 5 of this chapter.

1-43.caveats: Grade B is assigned because while trials conclusively prove that direct inquiry causes no harm, trials cannot ethically measure reductions in completed suicides. Benefit magnitude is rated Low because it reflects surrogate endpoints (ideation frequency rather than absolute mortality counts). Most trial protocols utilized clinical interviews or standardized screening questionnaires rather than informal peer conversations, though clinical guidelines generalize this finding to friends and family. If someone confirms they are having suicidal thoughts, do not leave them unattended: stay with them, connect them immediately to a crisis helpline (Tele-MANAS on 14416, or 112 if it is an emergency), and remove access to lethal means (medications, sharp objects, chemicals), as outlined in Chapter 1, Rule 25. If they express intent to harm others or have active preparations underway, immediate emergency services or hospital evaluation is necessary, as described in Chapter 8, Rule 15. The interval between acute ideation and action is often mere minutes, as noted in Chapter 1, Rule 32. Primary beneficiaries are family members, partners, friends, and colleagues.

1-20.title: People with cardiovascular disease and older adults should get a flu shot each year
1-20.cost: One shot costs about ₹2,500–₹3,200 at a private clinic, and government facilities charge less. It should be given once each autumn.
1-20.inPlainWords: In a trial involving people after a heart attack, the yearly death rate dropped from 4.9% to 2.9% after they received the flu vaccine. For people with cardiovascular disease and older adults, getting one shot each autumn for a few thousand rupees can make a real difference.
1-20.benefit: This trial included 2,571 participants after a myocardial infarction; neither doctors nor patients knew who got the vaccine or the placebo. Over 12 months, the overall death rate was 2.9% in the vaccine group versus 4.9% in the placebo group. The hazard ratio was 0.59, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.39 to 0.89. Cardiovascular death rates also showed a hazard ratio of 0.59. Another study pooled multiple trials and found that flu vaccination lowered the rate of major cardiovascular events to 3.6% from 5.4% in the control group; the relative risk was 0.66, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.53 to 0.83. Cardiovascular death risk showed a relative risk of 0.74, though this fell within the margin of error and was not statistically significant (95% CI 0.42 to 1.30).

1-42.benefit: Safety directives from the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety (CCOHS) and Workplace Health and Safety Queensland specify clear operating standards: inspect the protective guard and abrasive disc prior to operation; never use discs that are cracked, chipped, or warped. The maximum rated RPM marked on the disc must never be lower than the grinder's spindle speed. Ensure arbor size and disc diameter match manufacturer specifications precisely. Disconnect power before changing discs. Clamp workpieces securely before grinding or cutting. Wear safety glasses or goggles beneath a full-face shield. Maintain a balanced stance with both hands on the tool handles. Never use cutting discs for side-grinding, which causes structural disc failure. Do not put the tool down until the disc has come to a complete stop. Direct sparks and debris away from people and combustible materials. Queensland workplace alerts note that disc edge velocity typically reaches 70 meters per second; fitting a larger 356 mm disc onto a 230 mm tool elevates edge speed beyond 120 m/s, rapidly causing explosive disintegration. In February 2016, an Australian worker using a 230 mm angle grinder was fatally injured when projectile disc fragments penetrated his chest. Formal accident investigations in other jurisdictions record the same pattern: a toothed blade fitted where a disc belongs, the guard removed, and a fatal kickback. In India the limit comes from two places rather than one product standard: the tool's own instruction manual, which lists only the disc types and diameters that grinder is approved for — a saw chain, a wood-carving blade or a toothed saw blade is not among them — and residual current protection on the supply, for which IS 12640 (Part 2) is the Indian standard covering residual current operated circuit-breakers with integral overcurrent protection. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 requires an employer to provide a safe system of work, which is what a guard, a face shield and a two-handed grip amount to. Emergency department injury surveillance in South Korea between 2011 and 2018 tracked 8,697 injuries from high-speed rotating tools, with 4,603 cases caused by grinders: 46.4% sustained hand injuries and 23.0% suffered head/facial trauma. Compared to other rotating tools, angle grinders carried over twice the odds of severe injury (OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.88–2.29). In a hospital study of 36 patients with ocular grinder trauma, 10 sustained permanent post-surgical visual acuity below 0.05 (legal blindness). An orthopedic study of 742 acute forearm and hand injuries in Turkey found angle grinders responsible for 82 cases, of which 44% occurred among retirees doing DIY home repairs. A Japanese trauma series of 15 grinder injuries found 9 were caused by improper attachments such as woodworking blades, resulting in complete finger amputations.

1-44.benefit: AFib causes chaotic atrial quivering, leading to blood stasis and thrombus formation. The most common symptoms are palpitations, exertional fatigue, and chest discomfort, though approximately 25% of individuals report no noticeable symptoms. A single-lead ECG recording lasting >=30 seconds or a standard 12-lead ECG lasting >=10 seconds provides definitive diagnosis. A 2007 meta-analysis pooled 29 randomized controlled trials with 28,044 participants: compared to control/placebo, dose-adjusted warfarin reduced stroke by 64% (95% CI 49%–74%), whereas antiplatelet therapy (such as aspirin) reduced stroke by only 22% (95% CI 6%–35%). In direct head-to-head trials, warfarin reduced stroke by an additional 39% compared to antiplatelets. Absolute increase in major extracranial hemorrhage was under 0.3% per year. A Cochrane review evaluating 2,313 individuals with no prior stroke found warfarin lowered all-cause mortality by roughly 30% (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.50–0.94). Four landmark trials totaling 71,683 patients comparing direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) to warfarin demonstrated DOACs further reduced stroke and systemic embolism by 19% (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.73–0.90) and all-cause mortality by 10% (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.85–0.95), with a 52% reduction in intracranial hemorrhage (RR 0.48), despite a 25% increase in gastrointestinal bleeding (RR 1.25). Aspirin cannot replace anticoagulation: in 5,599 patients unsuitable for warfarin, apixaban reduced stroke and systemic embolism by 55% compared to aspirin (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.32–0.62) with no significant difference in major bleeding (1.4% vs 1.2% per year; HR 1.13, 95% CI 0.74–1.75). In the BAFTA trial of 973 seniors aged >=75, warfarin reduced fatal or disabling stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, or arterial embolism by 52% compared to aspirin (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.28–0.80) with similar extracranial bleeding (1.4% vs 1.6% per year). Guidelines explicitly advise against antiplatelet monotherapy for AFib stroke prevention. ACC/AHA 2023 guidelines emphasize anticoagulation decisions depend on thromboembolic risk, regardless of whether AFib is paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent, and bleeding scores should be used to address modifiable bleeding risks rather than inappropriately withhold anticoagulation. Indian data point the same way: in a community screening in Nagpur published in 2016, eight of 4,077 adults had atrial fibrillation, and of those eight only three were on warfarin — none with routine INR monitoring — while one was on aspirin. The authors concluded that stroke prophylaxis was underused.
1-44.inPlainWords: Atrial fibrillation (AFib) causes the heart's upper chambers to beat chaotically, allowing blood to pool and form clots; if a clot travels to the brain, it triggers a devastating ischemic stroke. Taking doctor-prescribed anticoagulants reduces the risk of stroke by roughly 60% and lowers overall mortality by about 30%. Antiplatelet drugs like aspirin reduce stroke risk by only about 20% and cannot serve as an effective substitute. In an Indian community screening published in 2016, only three of the eight people found to have AFib were on warfarin, and none had routine INR monitoring.

1-35.title: Don’t trade “losing one kidney is no big deal” for cash: the remaining kidney has to do the work of two, and 86% of kidney sellers later say their health got worse
1-35.cost: No cost at all. It simply requires a clear look at the facts.
1-35.inPlainWords: First, consider the best-case scenario: legitimate donors who pass rigorous screening and receive post‑surgery follow‑up. In U.S. data from nearly 96,000 donors, only 31 per 10,000 developed end‑stage renal disease within 15 years after donation. Among equally healthy, eligible non‑donors, that figure was just 4 per 10,000. On the other side, a study of 305 kidney sellers in India found that six years later, 86% reported poorer health, and three‑quarters still carried debt. Legitimate donors get screening and monitoring; kidney sellers get none of that.
1-35.benefit: U.S. researchers compared 96,217 living kidney donors with 20,024 similarly healthy non‑donors drawn from the NHANES III survey. After 15 years, the estimated risk of developing end‑stage renal disease (ESRD) was 30.8 per 10,000 donors (95% CI 24.3–38.5) versus 3.9 per 10,000 non‑donors (95% CI 0.8–8.9; P<0.001). Over a lifetime, ESRD risk was 90 per 10,000 donors, 14 per 10,000 non‑donors, and 326 per 10,000 in the general population. A Norwegian study of 1,901 donors (median follow‑up 15.1 years) showed a 30% higher overall mortality (HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.11–1.52), a 40% higher cardiovascular mortality (HR 1.40, 95% CI 1.03–1.91), and roughly tenfold higher ESRD risk (HR 11.38, 95% CI 4.37–29.6). Among 3,698 U.S. donors, 11 developed ESRD — an incidence of 180 per million person‑years, compared with 268 per million in the general population. Of those re‑examined after an average of 12.2 years, 255 remained healthy, and 85.5% retained a glomerular filtration rate of at least 60 ml/min/1.73 m², the clinical lower limit of normal. Hypertension affected 32.1% and proteinuria 12.7%. In Chennai, 305 people who had sold a kidney — surveyed in February 2001, an average of six years after the operation — had been paid an average of about ₹50,000 at February 2001 exchange rates (the study reported the sum in US dollars). 96% had sold to pay off debts. Family income fell by one third (P<0.001), poverty rose, three-quarters were still in debt, 86% said their health had worsened, and 79% would not recommend kidney selling to others.

1-35.caveats: Controversy exists: Ibrahim’s study used ordinary citizens as controls and found no difference in survival or ESRD risk between donors and non‑donors. Muzaale and Mjøen compared donors to equally healthy, eligible non‑donors and found markedly higher risks. The disagreement concerns the control group, not the donors themselves. All three studies agree that absolute risks remain low (30.8 per 10,000 over 15 years). Thus the key points are two: first, the remaining kidney does bear extra strain, as shown by higher rates of hypertension and proteinuria; second, these figures apply only to donors who undergo pre‑ and post‑operative screening and medical care — conditions absent for illegal kidney sellers, whose outcomes differ sharply according to Indian follow‑up data. Original studies provide only self‑reported health decline, proteinuria, hypertension, and ESRD rates; no figures on bed‑bound status are included here. Selling a kidney is a criminal offence in India under the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act, 1994, and the rules on who may lawfully donate at all are covered in Chapter 9, Item 22. Paying for long-term dialysis after your own kidneys fail is the harder problem, and the cover depends on which scheme you are in. Employees of establishments covered by the Employees' State Insurance Act get medical care for themselves and their families through ESIC dispensaries and hospitals, with referral for specialist treatment. Central government employees and pensioners use CGHS wellness centres and empanelled hospitals. Families on the eligible lists get ₹5 lakh a year of hospital cover under Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY; the National Health Authority says a beneficiary can be treated cashless at any empanelled hospital outside the home state, with the home state paying. Many states also run their own scheme for residents who are not on those lists. None of these pays at a private hospital of your choosing: the hospital has to be empanelled under the scheme that covers you, and job- or city-linked cover such as ESIC and CGHS has to be transferred when you move. Ask the hospital's scheme desk which cover it will accept before treatment starts.

1-38.cost: This is a prescription medication, so in most places it must be paid for out of pocket. Generic tenofovir/emtricitabine is made by several Indian manufacturers, and the monthly price varies with the brand and the pharmacy, so ask for the price of a 30-tablet pack before you start. Before prescribing it, doctors must test for HIV, kidney function, and hepatitis B. Follow-up tests are required every three months. The main challenge is remembering to take the pills every day without fail.
1-38.caveats: The participants in these trials were primarily men who have sex with men; therefore, they are the group most encouraged to seek this treatment. Others at high risk of infection can also consult doctors to determine suitability. Prior to prescribing, it is essential to confirm that patients are not already infected; taking the medication while infected can foster viral resistance. Self-test results cannot be used as a basis for prescription. For individuals with hepatitis B, discontinuing treatment may trigger a flare-up, so testing is mandatory beforehand. WHO currently recommends on-demand dosing only for men who have sex with men engaging in sex fewer than twice a week; the regimen involves taking two tablets 2–24 hours prior to sex, followed by one tablet 24 and 48 hours afterward. Women and hepatitis B carriers must adhere to daily dosing. Trials involving on-demand dosing reported more gastrointestinal and kidney-related side effects than placebo groups; hence, regular medical checkups are indispensable. In India, ask an Integrated Counselling and Testing Centre (ICTC) under the National AIDS and STD Control Programme: it will test you and refer you to the ART centre or clinic that prescribes PrEP. The National AIDS Helpline on 1097 is toll-free, runs 24×7, and can tell you where the nearest ICTC and ART centre are. Importantly, this medication does not protect against sexually transmitted infections such as syphilis or gonorrhea; condoms must still be used consistently, as noted in Section 30 of this chapter. In cases where exposure has already occurred, emergency post-exposure prophylaxis is available per Section 13, Item 38 (within 72 hours). Ultimately, this treatment safeguards both the individual and their sexual partners.
